history.dynasty: Built at the instance of Sheth Sri Motishah; consecrated at the instance of his son Sri Khimchandra (Kheemji) in Vikram Samvat 1893
history.summary: THIS IS A JAIN TEMPLE, NOT A HINDU TEMPLE — keep-or-drop decision needed. Motishah Tuk (tunk = a walled cluster of shrines) is one of the nine principal tunks on Shatrunjaya hill, Palitana, and is described as the biggest of the tunk temples: a cluster of large and small temples whose principal deity is Adinath (Adishvar Bhagwan). It was built by Seth Motishah (Moti Chand Shah, a Bombay-based Oswal Jain merchant and ship-owner, born at Bombay to Amin Chand of Khambhat) and, after his death in VS 1892 (1835), grandly consecrated (pratishta) by his son Seth Kheemji/Khimchandra on Magh Sudi 10, VS 1893 (1836 CE), at a reported cost of over Rs. 18 lakh of the time, with ~5,000 artistic Jain images carved for it. Related to seq 1510 and seq 1464 (same Shatrunjaya hill complex) but a distinct tunk, NOT a duplicate. Media image shows the hilltop Shatrunjaya temple cluster generally, not the Motishah Tuk specifically. Coordinates are for the hilltop complex — the exact tunk position is APPROXIMATE (verify).

name: Motishah Tuk
town_description: Palitana is a temple town in Bhavnagar district, Gujarat, about 55 km southwest of Bhavnagar city, at the foot of Shatrunjaya hill. It is one of the holiest pilgrimage centres of Jainism, hosting hundreds of marble Jain temples clustered on the hilltop, and draws pilgrims and visitors from across India and abroad, especially during the Kartik Purnima fair. It is a strictly vegetarian pilgrimage town served by its own railway terminus.

travel.airport: Bhavnagar Airport, approx. 55-65 km by road (verify); Ahmedabad approx. 215 km.
travel.railway: Palitana railway station (terminus on the Bhavnagar line); Bhavnagar Terminus approx. 55 km.
travel.road: Palitana lies on the Ahmedabad-Palitana road, approx. 50-55 km from Bhavnagar; buses and taxis available. Reaching the tunk requires the Shatrunjaya climb of ~3,500 steps.

visitor_information.best_time: October to March, when the weather suits the long early-morning climb.
visitor_information.opening_hours: Hill temples are typically open from early morning (around 6:00 AM) to evening; no tunk-specific hours found (verify with the Anandji Kalyanji Trust).
